sysadmin_function.title: Sysadmin 1 — The Sysadmin Function & the System Landscape
sysadmin_function.desc: The sysadmin function on the managed CloudERP.One platform: the custody map (site, apps, Desk, bench); the awesome bar; DocType grammar and the docstatus lifecycle; lists, saved filters, and the three report kinds; the System Settings walk with its three rules; workspace curation per job family with the click-count audit; the sysadmin calendar by frequency; and the five-item support report.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The sysadmin function on a managed platform
lessons.html:
This track certifies the system administrator: the person who owns the ZhiftERP machinery itself — its users and permissions, its master data governance, its backups, its changes, its channels, and its health. Every other track teaches operating a module; this one teaches operating the platform they all run on.

The division of custody. ZhiftERP on CloudERP.One is a managed platform, and the custody line must be learned on day one:

• The host (CloudERP.One) owns the infrastructure layer: the servers, the database engine, the platform updates, the off-site backup machinery, uptime, and the network. Problems at that layer are raised, not fixed locally — Chapter 8 covers the support channel and what a good report contains.
• The site sysadmin (this certification) owns everything inside the site: users, roles and permissions; System Settings and the module settings; master data governance; the backup verification habit; change control for customisations; email, printing, and integrations; and the monitoring reads.

The sysadmin owns the machinery, not the data: accounts policy belongs to the accountant, stock policy to the stock owner. The sysadmin makes their policies executable — a role built, a validation enabled, a setting recorded — and keeps the platform trustworthy underneath them.

Why the function is a named role. Systems without a named sysadmin all drift the same way: everyone is a System Manager because setup was easier that way; settings change per complaint and nobody knows when; masters duplicate; leavers keep logins; the backup has never been test-restored; and the first serious incident finds no owner. Every one of those is a module of this track, and the fix in every case begins the same way: one named person owns the machinery, with a named backstop.

What the role is not. Not a developer (customisations are governed in module 5, not written here), not the data's owner, and not a bottleneck — the whole design goal is a platform so well-governed that daily work never waits for the sysadmin.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the platform's anatomy — sites, apps, and the Desk. Chapter 3: DocTypes and documents — the system's grammar. Chapter 4: lists, filters, and reports. Chapter 5: the System Settings walk. Chapter 6: workspaces and the module map. Chapter 7: the sysadmin calendar. Chapter 8: the support channel and the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The platform's anatomy: site, apps, and the Desk
lessons.html:
Four terms carry the whole architecture. Learn them precisely — every support conversation and every module of this track uses them.

The site. The business's own installation: its database, its files, its users, its settings. One site is one business system, isolated from every other site on the platform. Everything this track governs lives inside the site.

The apps. The software the site runs: the framework (the engine — forms, permissions, reports, email), the ERP application (the business doctypes — Sales Invoice, Item, Journal Entry), and any extension apps the implementation added. The installed list is visible from Help > About — the versions shown there are the first thing the host's support asks for. Apps are code and belong to the host's update stream (module 5); the site's data and settings are the sysadmin's.

The Desk. The working interface at /app — workspaces on the left, the awesome bar (the search box at the top) as the fastest route to anything. Learn the awesome bar's three uses now, because this track's instructions lean on it:

1. Type a doctype's name to jump to its list — Sales Invoice opens the invoice list.
2. Type new plus a doctype to create — new user opens a blank User.
3. Type a settings or tool name to open it directly — System Settings, Role Permission Manager, Data Import.

The portal is the other face: the website side where customers, suppliers, or — in this platform's case — Duty Board rooms are served to non-Desk users. Chapter 2 of module 2 makes the Desk/portal distinction precise at the user level, because it decides both licensing and exposure.

The bench. The host-side machinery that runs sites: process management, scheduled jobs, updates, server backups. On the managed platform the bench is CloudERP.One's custody. The sysadmin needs the word because support conversations use it — the bench was updated, a bench job failed — and because module 4 and 5 describe what the host does there on the site's behalf.

The custody map, restated on the anatomy. Site data and settings: the sysadmin. App code and versions: the host's stream, received governed (module 5). The bench and below: the host, reached through the support channel with the About-page versions in hand.

Practical rule: when anything is reported broken, place it on this map first. "A user cannot see a report" is site custody (permissions — module 2). "The site is down" is bench custody (raise it, with the time and what changed). The map decides who moves.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — DocTypes and documents: the system's grammar
lessons.html:
Everything in ZhiftERP is a DocType — a form definition — and every record is a document of one. The sysadmin reads this grammar fluently, because permissions, imports, reports, and customisations all speak it.

The anatomy of a DocType. Open any document and read it as structure:

• Fields — each with a type (Data, Link, Select, Date, Currency, Table…). The type decides behaviour: a Link field points at another doctype's records (the Customer field on a Sales Invoice links to the Customer doctype), which is how the system stays consistent — you cannot invoice a customer who does not exist.
• Child tables — the rows inside a document (the Items table on an invoice) are themselves documents of a child doctype.
• Naming — every document has a unique name/ID, produced by its naming rule: a series (SINV-2026-00042), the field's own value (a Customer named by customer name), or a set format. Module 3 governs series properly.
• Mandatory and read-only markings, defaults, and validations — the form refusing a bad save is the permission layer's cousin: policy enforced at entry.

The document lifecycle — docstatus. Transaction doctypes carry three states, and the whole audit design of the system hangs on them:

• Draft (0) — editable, posts nothing. Draft sweeps at close (the Accounts track's cut-off) exist because drafts are invisible to the books.
• Submitted (1) — posted and locked. Submission is when a Sales Invoice writes its GL rows and stock moves. Submitted documents are not edited — the framework refuses it.
• Cancelled (2) — reversed, retained. Cancel posts the reversal and keeps the record; Amend creates the corrected successor linked to it. Nothing honest is ever deleted.

Master doctypes (Customer, Item, User) have no docstatus — they are current-state records, edited in place, with the audit trail carrying their history (module 8).

Standard versus custom. Standard doctypes and fields ship with the apps; Custom Fields and customisations are the site's own additions. The distinction matters twice: updates preserve customisations but standard structures may evolve under them (module 5's test discipline), and every custom field is a governance event — named, documented, owned — not a casual addition (module 5).

Practical rule: when a form behaves unexpectedly, read it as grammar before suspecting a fault — is the field a Link whose target is missing, a mandatory unfilled, a docstatus refusing edits? Most "bugs" reported to a sysadmin are the grammar working exactly as designed.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Lists, filters, and the report machinery
lessons.html:
The sysadmin answers most questions with a list view or a report, and teaches the business to answer its own. This chapter is that machinery.

List views. Every doctype's list (awesome bar → the doctype's name) carries the working toolkit:

• Filters — click Filter, or use the quick filters in the sidebar: Status = Draft, dated this month, by company, by owner. Filters chain — this is the close's draft sweep, the leaver's document check, the monthly journal review, all built from the same control.
• Sort, and the count. The list's count is itself a read — module 2's user reviews and module 7's health reads are lists counted.
• Saved filters — a filter set worth repeating is saved and named; it appears in the sidebar for one click next month. Routine reads (drafts this month, disabled users, failed emails) should all be one click by the end of this track.
• Bulk actions — select rows for bulk edit, assignment, or export. Powerful and therefore governed: bulk edit rights follow the same permission design as everything else (module 2).
• The report view — the list flipped into columns, with column choice, grouping, and totals. For most operational questions the report view of the right list is the report.

The three report kinds.

1. Report Builder reports — saved report views: columns, filters, sort, group-bys, built without code and shared by name. The sysadmin's default answer to "can we get a report of…" — built in minutes, owned by the asker.
2. Standard reports — the shipped analytical reports each module's track leans on (General Ledger, Stock Ledger, Accounts Receivable…). Script-driven, filter-rich, and drillable.
3. Custom query/script reports — code, and therefore module 5's territory: specified, tested, documented, owned. A business that jumps to custom reports before exhausting the first two kinds is buying maintenance it does not need.

Exports. Any list or report exports to spreadsheet. Two governance notes ride along: export permission is a real permission (module 2's matrix includes it — customer lists walk out of businesses as exports), and an exported spreadsheet is a snapshot that starts aging immediately — the standing answer to spreadsheet-first habits is the saved filter or report that reads live.

Practical rule: before building anything, ask which existing list answers the question. The sysadmin's craft is mostly knowing that the report already exists.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The System Settings walk
lessons.html:
Open System Settings (awesome bar). This is the site-wide policy page, and the sysadmin walks it exactly as the Accounts track walks Accounts Settings: each field read as the policy question it is, the answers recorded in the implementation file, changes after go-live as governed events, and an annual re-walk on the calendar.

The identity block. Country, time zone, date format, number format, first day of the week, and the float/currency precision. Set once at birth, correctly: the time zone stamps every document and log; the formats print on every invoice; precision inconsistencies produce permanent kobo-level reconciliation noise (the Accounts track meets this from the other side). Changing these mid-life is a governed event with a reason, not a preference toggle.

The session and login block. Session Expiry (idle sessions die — hours, not weeks, on a system holding the business's books), Allow Consecutive Login Attempts and the lockout window (brute force answered by the platform, not by hope), Allow Login Using Mobile Number / User Name (decide the identity story deliberately — email is the clean default), and the Forgot Password flow enabled so resets are self-service and logged instead of whispered to an admin.

The password block. Minimum Password Strength / Score enforced by the platform — the policy that works is the one users cannot decline. Module 8 completes this with two-factor authentication.

The files block. Maximum attachment size, and allowed file types where the platform exposes them. Attachments are evidence (every track attaches documents to entries), so the setting balances evidence habits against storage — and storage is a monitored number in module 7.

The backups line. The scheduled backup count kept on-site (module 4 owns the whole subject; the setting is noted on this walk so it is never a surprise).

The updates and notifications block. How the site learns of platform changes, and the email defaults that module 6 completes.

The walk's three rules — identical to every settings walk in the programme:

1. Every field is a policy question; the answer is written down with its reason.
2. Post-go-live changes are governed events — reason, record, and where user-facing, an announcement.
3. The annual walk is the routine occasion for change; complaint-driven toggling is how sites drift into states nobody can explain.

Practical rule: the recorded walk is the difference between settings and decisions. A site whose System Settings page can be read aloud with a reason per field passes this module's core test.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Workspaces and the module map
lessons.html:
The Desk's left sidebar is workspaces — the doors people walk through every day. The sysadmin curates them, because an uncurated Desk taxes every user every day.

What a workspace is. A configurable page of shortcuts, report links, and cards for one working domain: Accounting, Stock, Selling, HR. Users see the workspaces their roles and module access allow (module 2 wires this); within that, workspaces can be edited — shortcuts added, cards arranged — and custom workspaces created for job families.

Curation, as a procedure.

1. Per job family, list the daily objects: the cashier's four doctypes, the storekeeper's six, the accountant's dozen. The lists are short — that is the point.
2. Build or trim the workspace to the list: the daily doctypes and their New buttons as shortcuts, the role's two or three standing reports (Chapter 4's saved filters and Report Builder reports) linked by name, everything else removed from sight.
3. Hide the modules the role never uses — module 2's allowed-modules control per user — so the sidebar shows a person their own system, not the whole platform.
4. Review at the annual walk: shortcuts nobody clicks are removed; the new routine report earns its link.

Why this is a sysadmin duty and not decoration. Three concrete returns:

• Training cost. A new cashier facing four shortcuts learns in a day; one facing forty doctypes learns fear. Every onboarding in every track lands on the Desk the sysadmin curated.
• Error rate. People misfile into doctypes they can see but should not touch. The workspace that shows only the job's objects removes a whole error class before permissions even engage.
• Adoption. The system the owner reads from daily is the one whose workspace answers the owner's three questions on one screen — the statements, the cash position, the exceptions. Module 7 builds that read; the workspace is where it lives.

The module map. Alongside curation, the sysadmin keeps the one-page map of which modules the business actually runs — Accounts, Stock, Selling, Buying, HR, and the platform's own Duty Board — with each module's owner named. The map drives the allowed-modules defaults, the workspace set, and module 5's impact analysis (a change to Stock touches these people, this workspace, these reports).

Practical rule: audit the Desk from a new employee's seat once a year — log in as a test user of each job family and count the clicks to their daily work. More than two clicks to a daily object is a curation fault.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The sysadmin calendar
lessons.html:
The function runs on a calendar, like every governed function in this programme. Each line has a named owner and a written procedure; most lines are single-digit minutes once the routines settle.

Daily — the five-minute read (module 7 details each):

• The Error Log scanned — new error types investigated, known noise acknowledged.
• The email queue glanced — stuck outbound mail is business documents not arriving (module 6).
• The scheduled jobs confirmed running — a dead scheduler silently stops backups, emails, and auto-repeats.
• Yesterday's backup confirmed present (module 4's daily line).

Weekly:

• The user delta: new users, disabled users, role changes this week — read from the User list and reconciled against HR's joiner/leaver notes (module 2's lifecycle).
• The failed logins / lockouts read for patterns.
• Storage and performance numbers noted — trends, not points (module 7).

Monthly:

• The restore verification — module 4's law: a backup untested is a hope. One backup, restored to the test site, opened and read.
• The permission delta review — what changed in the Role Permission Manager this month, by whom, why (module 2).
• The master hygiene read — duplicate candidates, naming drift, orphaned records (module 3).
• The integration health check — every connected channel exercised or read (module 6).

Quarterly:

• The access recertification — every active user re-confirmed by their manager: right roles, right restrictions, still employed (module 2's strongest control).
• The update review — the host's release notes read against the site; the test-then-live cycle run for pending changes (module 5).
• The incident log read by cause — repeat causes are process faults.

Annually:

• The System Settings walk (Chapter 5) and the module settings walks with their owners.
• The security review — 2FA coverage, password policy, API keys and integration credentials rotated (module 8).
• The full continuity rehearsal — the restore drill at full dress (module 4).
• The workspace and Desk audit (Chapter 6) and the customisation register reconciled (module 5).

Practical rule: the calendar is the function. A sysadmin without one is a firefighter, and the fires pick the schedule — install the calendar in month one and let module 7's reads populate it.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The support channel & the HealthTrade case
lessons.html:
The support channel. Custody-map problems that belong to the host are raised through the CloudERP.One support channel — and the quality of the report decides the speed of the fix. A good report carries five things:

1. The site and the versions — from Help > About.
2. The exact time the problem started, with the time zone.
3. What changed — an update received, a setting changed, an import run, nothing known.
4. The reproduction — the steps that show it, the user it affects, the error text copied whole (and the matching Error Log entry — module 7 teaches reading it).
5. The scope — one user or all, one doctype or everywhere, constant or intermittent.

The sysadmin triages before raising: is it the custody map's site side (a permission, a setting, a filter) — fixed locally; or the platform side — raised with the five items. Both outcomes are logged in the incident book, because module 7's quarterly read mines that log for repeat causes.

The HealthTrade case — the function installed. HealthTrade arrives at this track as the other tracks left it: modules well-operated, and the platform beneath them owned by nobody — the implementation partner had been the accidental sysadmin, and the gap shows the standard symptoms: five System Managers, settings nobody can explain, an untested backup, and a Desk showing every user everything.

Month one — the function is named. The operations lead takes the role with the accountant as backstop; both are written into the policy page. The custody map is drawn on one page and taught in one meeting: what the business owns, what CloudERP.One owns, and the five-item report format for the boundary.

Month two — the ground is read. The About page is recorded. The System Settings walk runs field by field with answers written — session expiry tightened from the install default, the password score enforced, precision confirmed against the accounts setup. The module map is drawn with owners, and the first Desk audit runs from a test cashier login: eleven clicks to reach the till's daily documents. Workspace curation begins with the cashier and storekeeper families — the recount after: two clicks.

Month three — the calendar starts. The daily five-minute read begins (and catches, in its second week, a stuck email queue that module 6 will fix properly). The weekly user delta runs against HR's notes and finds two leavers still enabled — module 2's lifecycle procedure lands the same week, which is exactly where this track goes next.

The MD's note in the month-three file: the platform now has an owner, a map, and a schedule. The modules were always run well; now the thing they run on is run well too.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the first law
lessons.html:
The recurring platform-custody failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the unnamed function. Symptom: no one owns the machinery; every symptom in this chapter present at once; the implementation partner as accidental, absent sysadmin. Cause: the role never named (Chapter 1). Fix: one named owner with a named backstop, the custody map taught, the calendar started — the function exists the day those three exist.

Pattern 2 — settings by drift. Symptom: a System Settings page nobody can explain; formats and precision changed mid-life; session and password controls at install defaults years on. Cause: settings treated as toggles, changed per complaint, never recorded (Chapter 5). Fix: the recorded walk — every field a written decision — changes as governed events, and the annual re-walk as the only routine occasion.

Pattern 3 — the uncurated Desk. Symptom: every user seeing every module; new staff trained by fear; misfiled documents in doctypes nobody should have opened; the owner never reading the system because the system shows too much. Cause: workspaces never curated, modules never trimmed (Chapter 6). Fix: the per-job-family curation procedure, the allowed-modules defaults, and the annual test-login audit with its click count.

Pattern 4 — the spreadsheet shadow system. Symptom: exports everywhere; decisions made on snapshots days old; "the report" meaning a spreadsheet someone maintains by hand. Cause: the list/filter/report machinery never taught (Chapter 4). Fix: saved filters and Report Builder reports built with the askers, the live-versus-snapshot lesson taught, and export permission governed like the real permission it is.

Pattern 5 — the eloquent-symptom report. Symptom: platform issues reported as "it's not working", escalated with heat and no facts; fixes slow because diagnosis starts from zero. Cause: no report discipline (Chapter 8). Fix: the five-item format taught and templated — versions, time, what changed, reproduction with the whole error text, scope — and the incident book receiving every case, local or raised.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the custody map — site, apps, Desk, bench — and place any reported problem on it; use the awesome bar's three moves; read a doctype's grammar — fields, Link fields, child tables, naming — and the docstatus lifecycle with why nothing honest is deleted; build a filtered list, save it, flip it to report view, and name the three report kinds in escalation order; walk System Settings' blocks with the three rules; curate a workspace by the four-step procedure and defend the click-count audit; recite the calendar by frequency; and write a five-item support report.

The first law: the platform has a named owner — every setting is a written decision, and the machinery is governed like the books it carries. Module 2 opens the largest subject in the sysadmin's custody: users, roles, and permissions.

users_permissions.title: Sysadmin 2 — Users, Roles & Permissions
users_permissions.desc: Users, roles, and permissions in ZhiftERP: the User record and the System/Website User distinction; the joiner, mover, and leaver procedures — leavers disabled, never deleted; Role Profiles as jobs-as-objects with the two-System-Manager rule; the Role Permission Manager's actions, If Owner, and permission levels; User Permissions as record-level fences with Applicable For; share, assignment, and workflow kept distinct from permission; and the weekly delta, monthly permission delta, and quarterly access recertification.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The permission layer: policy as configuration
lessons.html:
Every control in every track of this programme — the journal pen's two names, the preparer/releaser split, the frozen-edit role, the write-off workflow — is, mechanically, a permission this module's machinery enforces. The sysadmin builds and maintains that machinery; the policy itself belongs to the function owners. This module covers the whole layer: the User record and its lifecycle, the Desk/portal user distinction, roles and Role Profiles, the Role Permission Manager, User Permissions for record-level restriction, sharing and assignment, the reviews that keep the layer honest, and the HealthTrade case.

The three questions the layer answers. Every access decision decomposes into three, and the system has a distinct mechanism for each:

1. Who are you? — the User record: identity, credentials, enabled or not (Chapters 2-3).
2. What may your job do? — Roles, granted in bundles by Role Profile, given force in the Role Permission Manager: which doctypes, which actions — read, write, create, submit, cancel, amend, delete, report, export (Chapters 4-5).
3. Which records may you do it to? — User Permissions: the row-level fence that confines a user to their company, their branch's cost centre, their warehouse (Chapter 6).

Access follows the job, never the person: the cashier role exists whether the cashier is Ada or Emeka, and people receive access by receiving jobs. The day the job ends, the access ends — Chapter 3's lifecycle makes that mechanical, and Chapter 8's reviews confirm quarterly that it stayed true after every joiner, mover, and leaver the year produced.

The two standing temptations, named now.

• Over-granting for convenience: "just make them System Manager so it works." Every module of every track has shown what one over-mighty account costs; this module is where the discipline is built instead.
• Under-maintaining: access granted correctly and then never reviewed — roles accreting as people move jobs, leavers surviving as enabled logins. Chapter 8's reviews exist for exactly this decay.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the User record and the Desk/portal distinction. Chapter 3: the user lifecycle — joiner, mover, leaver. Chapter 4: roles and Role Profiles. Chapter 5: the Role Permission Manager. Chapter 6: User Permissions. Chapter 7: sharing, assignment, and workflows. Chapter 8: the reviews. Chapter 9: the HealthTrade case. Chapter 10: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The User record and the two user kinds
lessons.html:
Open a User record (awesome bar → new user, or the User list). Every person in the system is one of these, and the record's fields carry the identity policy.

The identity fields.

• Email — the username. One person, one address, always individual: shared logins are the layer's first mortal sin, because every control downstream — permissions, audit trails, approvals, the leaver procedure — assumes the account is a person. A shared "cashier@" login makes every till variance unattributable and every audit trail a shrug.
• Full Name — as documents will show it: approvals, audit trails, and assignments all print this name.
• Enabled — the life switch. Chapter 3's leaver procedure is this checkbox, cleared, the same day.

The two user kinds — User Type.

• System User — works on the Desk: the staff who create documents, run reports, operate modules. System Users consume Desk capacity and carry the full permission machinery of this module.
• Website User — portal-only: customers, suppliers, and portal-side participants see their own documents through the website face, never the Desk. On this platform, Duty Board room participants are the standing example. Website Users cost no Desk capacity and are confined by design to their own records.

The distinction is both a security boundary and a licensing decision: the review question "does this person need the Desk?" is asked at every joiner and every quarterly review, and the answer changes the User Type, not just the roles.

The access blocks on the record.

• Roles — granted via Role Profile (Chapter 4); the individual checkboxes below it are read, not hand-ticked.
• Allowed Modules — the sidebar trim from module 1's Desk curation: modules unticked disappear from the user's Desk.
• Defaults — the user's default company and similar values, cutting daily keystrokes and mis-posts.

The security block. Password set by the user through the reset flow (the admin never knows it — resets are self-service and logged, per module 1's settings); last login visible on the list (Chapter 8 reads it); two-factor enrolment where enforced (module 8); and API access keys existing only where an integration justifies them (module 6 governs those credentials).

Practical rule: the User list, filtered and counted, is the layer's first health read — Enabled = Yes is the real population; System Users are the Desk population; both counts belong in the monthly review.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The user lifecycle: joiner, mover, leaver
lessons.html:
Accounts are events, not favours. Three procedures cover the lifecycle, each triggered by an HR event, each logged.

The joiner, as a procedure.

1. The trigger is HR's confirmation — role, manager, start date, branch. No account exists before its trigger.
2. Create the User: individual email, Full Name as documents will print it, User Type answered deliberately (Desk or portal).
3. Grant the job, not permissions: attach the job family's Role Profile (Chapter 4), set Allowed Modules to the family's map, set the defaults (company, branch values), and apply the family's User Permissions (Chapter 6) — the Ibadan cashier confined to Ibadan from the first login.
4. First login through the reset flow — the admin never holds the password.
5. Log the grant: who, what profile, on whose authorisation, dated. Chapter 8's reviews read this log.

The mover — the procedure everyone forgets. When a person changes jobs, access must move, not accumulate:

1. The old Role Profile and User Permissions are removed the day the new ones are granted — one action, not two months apart.
2. The exception — a transition period where both are genuinely needed — is time-boxed in the log with an expiry date, and the expiry is honoured.

Unmanaged movers produce the classic audit finding: the accounts officer who was once a storekeeper and can still post stock. Every mover event is a diff: granted, removed, dated.

The leaver — same day, every time.

1. The trigger is HR's leaving date — for terminations, the hour, coordinated in advance.
2. Enabled is cleared on the User record. Never delete: the user's name is woven through the audit trail, approvals, and document ownership — deletion orphans history. Disabled preserves everything and permits nothing.
3. Sessions are revoked (the disable kills them; confirm), and any API keys on the record are revoked explicitly.
4. The person's open items are re-homed: assignments reassigned, workflow approvals redirected, saved reports and recurring notifications reviewed for ownership.
5. The departure joins the same-day checklist the whole programme shares: the bank mandate purge (Accounts track), the door codes, and this — the login. One leaver list, several owners, one date.

Practical rule: the weekly user delta (module 1's calendar) reconciles the User list against HR's events — every joiner has a log line, every mover a diff, every leaver a cleared checkbox dated to their last day.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Roles and Role Profiles
lessons.html:
A Role is a named capability set — Sales User, Stock Manager, Accounts User. A user holds roles; the Role Permission Manager (Chapter 5) decides what each role may do. This chapter is the design layer: which roles exist and how they are granted.

Standard roles first. The apps ship with a working role set per module — Sales User and Sales Manager, Stock User and Stock Manager, Accounts User and Accounts Manager, HR User, Purchase User, and the platform roles (System Manager above all). Use them as the base vocabulary: they are already wired to the doctypes, and the tracks' controls are expressed in them. Custom roles are created only when a real job family's needs match no standard role — and each custom role is a governed object: named for the job, documented, owned.

System Manager — the root of the layer. The role that administers users, permissions, and settings. The rule is absolute: two named holders at most — the sysadmin and the backstop — and it appears in no Role Profile. Every excess System Manager is a person who can quietly widen their own access; the count is read at every review, and the target is two.

Role Profiles — jobs as objects. Open Role Profile (awesome bar): a named bundle of roles representing one job family — Cashier, Storekeeper, Branch Manager, Accounts Officer. Attach the profile on the User record and the user holds exactly the bundle.

Why profiles instead of hand-ticked roles:

1. Consistency — every cashier holds the same set; the fifth cashier cannot be accidentally mightier than the first.
2. Speed — the joiner procedure is one attachment, not thirty checkboxes.
3. Reviewability — the quarterly review reads a short list of profiles instead of every user's checkbox forest; a person whose roles differ from their profile is by definition an exception with a story.
4. Change control — when the job family's needs change, the profile changes once and the change is a governed, logged event affecting a known population.

The design procedure. List the job families (module 1's module map already names them); for each, list the roles the family's daily work requires — the minimum set that lets the job run without borrowing; build the profile; and record, per profile, its Allowed Modules default and its standard User Permissions (Chapter 6). The complete set for a trading business is typically six to ten profiles — a one-page document that is, in effect, the access policy.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The Role Permission Manager
lessons.html:
Open the Role Permission Manager (awesome bar). This screen is where roles get their force: for each doctype, for each role, which actions are permitted. It is the single most consequential screen in the sysadmin's custody.

Reading the screen. Select a doctype — Sales Invoice. The rows are roles; the columns are actions:

• Read / Write / Create — see, edit drafts, make new.
• Submit / Cancel / Amend — the docstatus powers: post to the books, reverse, correct. These are the consequential three on every transaction doctype — a role with Create but not Submit prepares documents someone else posts, which is exactly how preparer/approver splits are built.
• Delete — kept off transaction doctypes for daily roles everywhere; the Accounts track's equity pattern is largely deletions.
• Report / Export / Print / Email / Share / Import — the movement-of-data actions. Export and Import are real controls: customer lists leave businesses as exports, and Import can create records at scale (module 3 governs it).
• If Owner — the permission applies only to documents the user created: the self-service pattern (staff read their own claims, not everyone's).

Permission levels. Beside level 0 (the document), fields can carry levels 1-9, and a role's grant at a level opens exactly those fields. The working use is surgical: the sensitive field family — a cost or margin field, a credit limit — set to level 1, and level-1 read/write granted only to the roles that own it. Powerful; used sparingly; every use documented, because an undocumented level scheme is a puzzle for the next sysadmin.

The design rules.

1. Change roles, not users. The manager grants to roles; a person needing more is a person whose profile is wrong or whose exception must be logged.
2. Least privilege, stated positively: each role holds what its job's daily work requires — the test is the job's task list, not the loudest request.
3. The programme's controls are non-negotiable grants: the Journal Entry pen at two names; Payment Entry submit split from preparation; the frozen-edit role disjoint from daily recorders; Delete off transactions; write-off behind its workflow. The sysadmin maintains these as the standing floor.
4. Every change is an event: what, who, why, when — the permission log Chapter 8 reviews monthly. The manager's power is exactly why its history must be boring.

Practical rule: when asked to "just give access", translate the request into role language aloud — which role, which doctype, which action, for which job reason. Requests that survive translation are granted to the role; requests that cannot name a job reason have answered themselves.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — User Permissions: the record-level fence
lessons.html:
Roles decide what a job may do; User Permissions decide which records it may do it to. This is the mechanism that confines the Ibadan cashier to Ibadan while the network runs one site.

What a User Permission is. Open User Permissions (awesome bar): each record is one fence — a user, a doctype, and an allowed value. User: ada@…, Allow: Cost Center, Value: Ibadan. With that fence in place, Ada's lists, reports, links, and new documents are confined to records carrying the Ibadan cost centre; other branches' documents neither open nor appear.

The working fences at a trading business.

• Company — the first fence on any multi-company site: each entity's staff confined to their entity (the Accounts track's legal-separation rule, enforced here).
• Cost Center / Branch — branch staff confined to their branch's documents and reads.
• Warehouse — storekeepers confined to their own stock locations.
• Customer / Supplier / Territory — where account ownership matters: a rep confined to their book.

The mechanics that matter.

1. Fences apply through Link fields: the permission on Cost Center confines every doctype whose documents carry that cost centre. One fence, network-wide effect.
2. Applicability can be narrowed: a fence can be set to apply only for specific doctypes (the "Applicable For" setting) — the surgical version, used when a full fence would block legitimate cross-branch reads.
3. Defaults cooperate: the fenced value doubles as the user's default — Ada's new documents are born at Ibadan, which is module 6-of-Accounts' addressing discipline enforced at the person.
4. Managers span by design: the branch manager's fence lists their branch; the operations lead has no branch fence at all. Absence of a fence is itself a decision — recorded, like every access decision.

The standard failure modes.

• The forgotten fence: the joiner procedure granted the profile but skipped the User Permission — the Ibadan cashier who can read Lagos. The profile document (Chapter 4) lists the family's standard fences precisely so this step cannot be skipped silently.
• The over-tight fence: a fence blocking a legitimate workflow (the cashier who cannot select the shared distribution warehouse). Diagnosed exactly like a permission issue — reproduce, read the fence list, narrow with Applicable For rather than deleting the fence.
• The stale fence after a move: Chapter 3's mover diff includes User Permissions, always.

Practical rule: fences are listed per user on the User Permissions list — filter by user and read it aloud at every mover event and every quarterly review. The fence list is the person's territory, stated in records.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Sharing, assignment, and workflow
lessons.html:
Three mechanisms sit beside the permission layer and are routinely confused with it. The sysadmin keeps them distinct, because each confusion is a control quietly bypassed.

Sharing. The Share button on any document grants one user access to one document — read, write, or share — regardless of their roles and fences. Its lawful use is the genuine exception: the auditor shown one contested invoice, the adviser shown one contract. Its abuse is permissions-by-share: access requests answered with shares until the permission design is a fiction nobody can review. Two rules: shares are exceptional and temporary (revoked when the reason ends), and the share list is readable per document — a document with many shares is a permission design failure surfacing as workaround.

Assignment. The Assign action (the ToDo it creates) routes work, not access: "this document is yours to action." Assignment grants nothing — the assignee still needs permission to open what they are assigned. The distinction runs both directions: assigning a document to someone without access produces the classic confused support ticket (the fix is the role or fence, not the assignment); and granting access because someone was assigned once inverts the design. Work routes by assignment; access follows the job.

Workflow. The Workflow doctype turns a document's path into governed states — Draft → Pending Approval → Approved — with each transition owned by a role and the document locked to its state's rules. This is the machinery behind every approval control in the programme: the journal threshold, the write-off's two signatures, the discount approval. The sysadmin's duties around workflows are specific:

1. Build to the owner's policy — the states, the transition roles, the thresholds come from the function owner; the sysadmin implements and documents them.
2. Keep transition roles aligned with the separation design — an approval state whose transition role includes the preparer's role has quietly collapsed a control (the Accounts track's rubber-stamp finding, seen from the build side).
3. Watch the workflow's health numbers — documents aging in a pending state mean an absent approver or a broken routing; approval times near zero mean rubber-stamping. Both reads land in module 7's monitoring and the CSA.
4. Change workflows as governed events — a workflow edit changes who can move money or seal figures, and is logged like the permission change it is.

Practical rule: when an access request arrives, name the mechanism before acting — is this a job (role), a territory (fence), one document (share), a task (assignment), or an approval path (workflow)? Five different answers, five different tools, and the discipline of naming prevents the quiet substitutions.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The reviews: keeping the layer honest
lessons.html:
Granted correctly is half the layer; still correct is the other half. Three reviews at three cadences, each a written procedure with an owner and an artifact.

Weekly — the user delta (five minutes). From module 1's calendar: the User list read for the week's changes — new users, disabled users, User Type changes — reconciled against HR's joiner/mover/leaver notes. Every difference is worked the same week: the joiner without a log line, the leaver still enabled, the mover without a diff. The artifact: one line in the ops log.

Monthly — the permission delta (fifteen minutes). What changed in the layer this month:

1. Role Permission Manager changes — each with its what/who/why from the permission log; any change without a log entry is itself the finding.
2. Role Profile edits — governed events affecting known populations; confirm the announcement went to affected owners.
3. New shares read per Chapter 7 — exceptional, temporary, reasons attached.
4. The System Manager count — the standing target of two, read every month without exception.

Quarterly — the access recertification (the strongest control in the module).

1. Export the population: every enabled user with their profile, roles, fences, User Type, and last login.
2. Split by manager: each manager receives their people's one-page access statements.
3. The manager certifies each line: right person, right profile, right territory, still employed, still needs the Desk — or names the change.
4. Changes are executed as mover events (the diff, logged); certifications are filed as the quarter's artifact.
5. The exceptions read: users whose roles differ from their profile (each must carry its logged story), users with no login in ninety days (candidates for disabling — the account nobody uses is pure risk), and any user holding more than one profile.

Why recertification works when everything else decays. It reverses the burden of proof: instead of the sysadmin noticing wrong access, every manager must positively confirm right access, on a schedule, in writing. Access decay — the mover's accretion, the forgotten contractor, the pilot-project role nobody removed — cannot survive four cycles of it. It is also the audit's favourite artifact: a year of certified quarters answers the access questions before they are asked.

Practical rule: the three reviews are cheap precisely because the machinery is clean — profiles make the population readable, logs make changes explainable, fences make territories printable. Reviews that hurt are diagnosing the layer, not the review.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: HealthTrade's access year
lessons.html:
The permission layer, rebuilt in one quarter and reviewed for a year. Every chapter appears.

The ground, as found. Module 1's audit closes with the layer's inventory: 19 enabled users, five holding System Manager (the MD, the accountant, the implementation partner's two old accounts, and a branch manager who "needed a report once"), two leavers enabled, one shared login — pharmacy@ — operating an entire branch counter, roles hand-ticked per user with no two cashiers alike, and no User Permissions at all: every branch could read every branch.

Week one — the stop-loss. The two leavers are disabled the same day (Chapter 3's procedure, run retroactively, with their open assignments re-homed). The implementation partner's accounts are disabled with the firm's confirmation. System Manager comes down to two named holders — the operations lead (the new sysadmin) and the accountant backstop — and the branch manager's "report" need is met properly with a Report Builder report shared to his role.

Weeks two to four — jobs as objects. The job families are listed with the module map: seven Role Profiles — Cashier, Pharmacist-Counter, Storekeeper, Branch Manager, Accounts Officer, Procurement Officer, Operations. Each profile is built from standard roles, documented with its Allowed Modules and standard fences, and attached user by user — the hand-ticked forests replaced in an afternoon per branch. The shared pharmacy@ login is retired: its two operators get individual accounts (Chapter 2's first mortal sin, corrected), and the next till variance at that counter is attributable for the first time.

Week five — the fences. User Permissions land per the profile documents: Cost Center fences for branch staff, Warehouse fences for the storekeepers, no fences for Operations by recorded decision. The Ibadan cashier's list views shrink to Ibadan overnight — and one over-tight fence surfaces within days (a cashier blocked from the shared distribution warehouse), narrowed with Applicable For rather than removed, exactly per Chapter 6.

The reviews begin. The weekly delta starts finding its ordinary catches (a joiner granted before HR's confirmation — reversed, then granted on the trigger). The first monthly permission delta reads clean except one Role Permission Manager change without a log line — the accountant, adding Export to a role for a year-end task; the change is logged retroactively and time-boxed. The first quarterly recertification mails seven managers their people's access statements and returns two findings: a mover still holding storekeeper roles four months after joining accounts (the classic — removed as a dated diff), and three ninety-day-no-login accounts (two disabled; one confirmed as a seasonal role and documented).

The year's numbers. System Managers: two, all four quarters. Recertification: four cycles filed. Shared logins: zero. Leavers enabled at review: zero after Q1. The auditor's access-controls section, previously two pages of findings, closes in one paragraph.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Common mistakes & the second law
lessons.html:
The permission layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the System Manager inflation. Symptom: five, eight, a dozen System Managers; "it was easier during setup"; anyone able to widen anyone's access. Cause: convenience never dismantled (Chapters 4-5). Fix: the count brought to two named holders, the role removed from every profile, and the monthly count read as a standing line.

Pattern 2 — the shared login. Symptom: counter@, store@, accounts@ — one password, several humans; variances unattributable; audit trails naming a mailbox. Cause: accounts treated as furniture instead of identities (Chapter 2). Fix: individual accounts for every human, the shared login retired with a date, and the attribution payoff taught with the first attributable variance.

Pattern 3 — access accretion. Symptom: long-tenured staff holding the union of every job they ever had; the accounts officer who can still post stock. Cause: movers granted-to without being removed-from (Chapter 3). Fix: the mover diff as a single event, time-boxed exceptions with honoured expiries, and the quarterly recertification catching what the diffs miss.

Pattern 4 — permissions by share. Symptom: documents carrying long share lists; access requests answered per-document for years; the Role Permission Manager describing a fiction. Cause: the exception mechanism used as the design (Chapter 7). Fix: shares audited and revoked to genuine exceptions, the underlying role/fence gaps fixed properly, and the monthly share read keeping it so.

Pattern 5 — the fenceless multi-branch site. Symptom: every branch reading every branch; reps browsing each other's customers; "confidential" meaning "please don't look". Cause: roles built, User Permissions never (Chapter 6). Fix: the fences installed per the profile documents — Company, Cost Center, Warehouse, party where owed — with recorded no-fence decisions for the spanning roles.

Pattern 6 — the unreviewed layer. Symptom: everything above, discovered years late, usually by an auditor. Cause: granted-then-forgotten (Chapter 8). Fix: the three cadences installed — weekly delta, monthly permission delta, quarterly recertification — each with its artifact filed.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the three questions and their mechanisms (User, Role/Role Profile + Role Permission Manager, User Permissions); create a user correctly and distinguish System from Website Users; run the joiner, mover, and leaver procedures — including why leavers are disabled, never deleted; design a Role Profile set and defend the two-System-Manager rule; read and change the Role Permission Manager by the four design rules, including Submit/Cancel/Amend, Delete off transactions, If Owner, and permission levels; build the four working fences and narrow one with Applicable For; distinguish share, assignment, and workflow from permission; and run the three reviews with their artifacts.

The second law: access follows the job — granted by profile, fenced by record, logged as events, and removed the day the job ends. Module 3 opens master data governance: the registers the whole system links to.
